en: The Sūtra on the Great Skillful Means Spoken by the Bodhisattva Prajñottara, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...

He was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering eight thousand—all of whom were great disciples fully perfected in the training—and twelve thousand bodhisattvas. All were masters of the holy penetrations, reaching everywhere without obstruction; they had attained dhāraṇī and immeasurable eloquence, as well as the patience of the non-arising of phenomena. Their virtues were boundless, and they perceived the faculties of others through and through. Bestowing medicine according to the ailment, they roared the lion’s roar, rescuing and delivering beings throughout the ten directions; among hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, there were none who did not receive deliverance.
At that time, not long after the World-Honored One had arisen from his meditative seclusion, he sat surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of followers as he preached the sutra.
Then, a bodhisattva in the assembly named Huisang rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; if the Tathāgata, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One, would deign to listen, I would venture to speak."
The World-Honored One said:
“Ask whatever you wish; the Buddha shall resolve your doubts and untie your entanglements.
Huisang addressed the Buddha:
"What is meant by 'skillful means' (upāya-kauśalya)?
The Buddha told Hui-shang:
"Excellent, excellent!"

"Noble son! Out of great compassion and pity, you take pity upon and seek the peace and security of the devas and humans; you exhort and transform those yet to come, guiding them away from the three miserable realms; you have expounded the Buddha-dharma and attained subtle and wondrous wisdom—therefore, you inquire about the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)."
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!"
"I shall now expound the essentials for you.
Bodhisattva Hui-shang and the assembled multitude received the instruction and listened attentively.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Hui-shang, saying:
“Son of good family!

A bodhisattva of skillful means, using a single portion of food, employs timely expedients to bestow it widely and universally. He exhorts and inspires those among the common people who have fallen into the state of animals, causing these two classes of beings to all turn toward the root of virtue and give rise to the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms, their minds becoming clear and fully endowed with the Buddha-wisdom.”
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva who possesses skillful means plants roots of virtue, encourages others, praises them, and rejoices in their merit, he dedicates these roots of goodness to all sentient beings.
With a mind of awakening, one accords with all minds without falling away.
Having expounded this teaching, the disciples are established; the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas serves as the basis for all-encompassing wisdom.
This is called the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, son of good family!

When the flowers of the various trees throughout the ten directions are brilliantly radiant, their fragrance is so exquisite that people hold them in high esteem, yet they have no known owner or name, the skillful bodhisattva respectfully gathers and collects them to scatter as offerings before the Buddhas. He vows that by virtue of this root of merit, he and all sentient beings may set their minds upon universal wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), thereby perfecting the light of the Way and fully attaining the immeasurable categories of morality (*śīla-skandha*), concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), liberation (*vimukti-skandha*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana-skandha*).
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Furthermore, son of good family, the bodhisattva of skillful means compassionately observes all sentient beings;

he rejoices in their well-being and undergoes their suffering on their behalf. By means of the causal conditions of various supernormal knowledges and wisdom, he establishes the roots of virtue to bestow upon all classes of beings. For the sake of the worlds of the ten directions, he vows to don the armor of virtue; when encountering those who suffer harm, he gathers them in for protection, undergoes their suffering on their behalf, and exhorts them with supernormal knowledge and wisdom so that they may attain great peace.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). Furthermore, son of good family,

when a bodhisattva who possesses skillful means makes offerings to a single Tathāgata, he contemplates that the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is equal, and that their categories of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*) are likewise so.

To know that making offerings to one Tathāgata is equivalent to honoring all Buddhas of the ten directions, and to perceive that the blessings and rewards received thereby are experienced by the Bodhisattvas as they successively bestow them upon sentient beings.
This is called the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, son of good family,
wherever a bodhisattva of skillful means is born, and in whatever place he dwells, he does not conceive of a self, nor does he ever disparage himself.
If one causes others to recite a four-line verse, observing its meaning with a mind that is neither timid nor weak, proclaiming it fully and clearly without thinking of gain or sustenance,

they shall cover all Buddha-lands. If they enter a kingdom or a city, they should immediately give rise to great compassion and joyfully expound it, vowing that all who hear these four lines of my verse shall attain the unimpeded eloquence of all Buddhas.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Furthermore, son of good family,

if a bodhisattva of skillful means is born into a household of poverty and must beg for a single evening's meal, he does not harbor a base or inferior mind, but instead offers it to the assembly of the worthy.

If one who is alone reflects within themselves, they will see that the Tathāgata has spoken of the necessity of expanding and broadening one's giving; yet now, what I have offered in alms is but meager and slight.

Having established the vow for universal wisdom and immeasurable resolve, I plant these roots of merit to inspire and awaken all sentient beings, hoping to obtain a precious palm like that of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
By means of this light of wondrous wisdom, one protects the evening offering; those who receive and wear it uphold the precepts and study the Way, thereby honoring merit and achieving much.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva of skillful means (upāyakauśalya) may travel together with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet his mind does not share their same destination;
when he sees people making offerings to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, his heart feels no sense of reverence or attainment therein."
It arises from two thoughts:
first, that one attains the state of a World-Honored Buddha from the mind of a bodhisattva;
second, that disciples and pratyekabuddhas are born from the Buddha-dharma.

Having formed this contemplation, one regards all offerings as not yet supreme; rather, that which I have studied—the threefold [wisdom]—is the most excellent. One contemplates it without partiality and without craving or delight.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva practicing skillful means performs a single act of giving, he thereby fulfills the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
What are the six perfections?
When a bodhisattva of skillful means encounters a poor beggar, he practices great giving with a heart free from stinginess or greed; this is the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).

He personally guards the prohibitions and upholds the precepts, while leading those who have committed evil to establish themselves in the Dharma of the precepts; he immediately bestows gifts upon them so that they may not further transgress; this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).

If there are those who harbor anger, one should govern them with a mind of loving-kindness, a pure mind, a luminous mind, and a mind of compassion; by thus giving rise to the practice of giving, this is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Providing meals and offerings as appropriate, with the actions of body, speech, and mind equal to space—this is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
Bestowing gifts with single-minded equanimity, remaining undisturbed in movement, stillness, sleep, and dreams—this is the perfection of concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).
Having given in this manner, one should contemplate all phenomena: who is there that gives?
What is it that is eaten?
Who is there that receives the retribution?

For one who acts thus seeking [this state], no dharma can be apprehended; one does not perceive a giver nor one who receives the gift of food, and there is no receiving of karmic retribution—this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), O son of good family!
"If one practices such provisional giving, then one is fully endowed with the dharmas of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Prajñottara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is unprecedented, O God among Gods!"

"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is fully endowed with the power of skillful means; he extensively protects and sustains all Buddha-dharmas, rescuing those in birth and death and extending his aid to other classes of beings.
The Buddha said: "How sublime!"
It is exactly as you have said.
Although the provisional bestowal is slight, if examined closely, it accomplishes immeasurable and incalculable multitudes of virtues.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Regarding the bodhisattva who practices skillful means (*upāya*), what is meant by "retreating"?

It is when one employs skillful means to give and bestow gifts, yet happens to be constrained by following evil friends. Having fully atoned for their transgressions, they reflect to themselves, saying:

"The aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) must all be extinguished; I shall eliminate these afflictions and reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). I vow to don the armor of the Way and virtue, exerting my strength to persevere from beginning to end, striving for ultimate realization."
Huishang asked again: "O Heaven among Heavens!
Suppose there were someone who had committed the four grave offenses, yet harbored certain thoughts and resolved to leave the household life for the sake of the bodhisattva path."
"What then? the Buddha said,
"Should one happen to violate the four grave prohibitions, by employing skillful means (*upāya*) to extinguish the transgressions, all afflictions will be entirely eliminated."
"O son of noble family!
For one who practices the path of a bodhisattva, there is no fault or transgression.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prajñottara addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva having transgressions and calamities?
The Buddha said:

"If there is a bodhisattva who studies and attains the *mokṣa-dharma* (precepts for liberation), one who has attained these precepts observes two hundred and fifty prohibitions; for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he subsists on fruits and gourds, enduring all insults from others."
If a bodhisattva harbors thoughts regarding the practices of disciples or pratyekabuddhas, he is then bound by the roots of birth and death.
O son of good family!
Just as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas violate their fundamental prohibitions, fail to eliminate the seeds of the aggregates (skandhas) and the sense-bases (āyatanas), and thus do not attain nirvāṇa.
O son of good family!

If one abandons the practices of a bodhisattva without correcting oneself, yet harbors thoughts of seeking the path of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, while wishing to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to become a most perfectly awakened one, one will ultimately never achieve it.
Thereupon Ānanda said to the World-Honored One:
"I recall that once, when I had entered the city of Śrāvastī to go on almsround, I saw a bodhisattva named Ghanarāja sitting upon a couch in another's chamber together with a woman."
I thought that I had committed an impurity and reflected in my mind:
"Could it be that some other person practicing the holy life has, within the teaching of the Tathāgata, perhaps produced views, perceptions, or mental conceptions regarding anything at all?"
"At that time, World-Honored One, as you beheld me standing in contemplation and uttered these words, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Then King Prasenajit immediately leaped into the air, staying four *zhang* and nine *chi* above the ground, and addressed Ānanda, saying:
'What is it, worthy one?'"
How could one who has committed a transgression and is defiled leap into the void and stop there?
Why did you not ask this before the Tathāgata?
What is meant by the dharma of a bodhisattva committing an offense?
Ānanda threw himself down and immediately repented his transgression, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One! I was utterly deluded and mistaken;
how could I have held such a biased view as to seek out the faults of the Great Dragon?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You should cultivate self-restraint and vigilance; do not look for the shortcomings of a Mahāyāna righteous person (saddharmasatva) by seeking their weaknesses. Just as when a worthy one is resolved upon the vehicle of the disciples (śrāvakayāna), even if one or two practice various mixed deeds together, you should not view them with suspicion or negligence, lest they fail to exhaust the outflows (āsrava)."
Thus it is, Ānanda!
Do not entertain the thought that a bodhisattva of skillful means can ever fall back from the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms. Why is this?

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through the karma of affectionately embracing his retinue, honors the Three Jewels—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the assembly of noble sages—and does not contravene them, thereby causing their wills to be set upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If sons or daughters of good family set their minds upon the Mahāyāna, do not depart from the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms, do not become distracted by the five pleasures but restrain the five desires, and contemplate the five supernormal powers to attain the faculties of a Tathāgata—then one should know that such a true person may dwell together with women."
Listen further, Ānanda!

That woman was the consort of King Saṃjaya for a hundred lifetimes in the distant past. Because her lingering affection had not been severed, she felt a bond of physical attachment; out of greed for Saṃjaya’s countenance, she made this vow:
"If I may enjoy my pleasures together with him, I shall follow his instruction and resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."

At that time, King Gaurīśrī, knowing her thoughts in his heart, appeared at dawn, adjusted his robes, and entered her chamber by means of this Dharma-gate. Observing that the internal and external realms were equal and devoid of grasping, he took her hand and dwelt with her as she desired.
Thus the verse says:
"Foolish indeed is the rebellion against desire, which the Buddhas do not praise;
one who can eliminate affection and craving attains Buddhahood, the highest among men."

At that time, the woman was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; she rose from her seat, threw herself upon the ground, took refuge, reproached herself, prostrated in confession of her faults, and offered this eulogy in praise of King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra:
“I have already distanced myself from all desires, as praised by the World-Honored One;
having restrained my attachment to affection and love, I pray for the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.”
"What my previous mind conceived, I now, with my own head, repent of my transgressions;
moved by compassion for all living beings, I have ultimately resolved to seek the Way.

At that time, the Bodhisattva King Reṣṭha, having transformed the woman according to her wishes and caused her to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true Way, rose from his seat and departed from the chamber.

Ānanda, observe how this mind maintains such purity; I now bestow upon this woman the prediction of enlightenment. After she transforms her female body, ninety-nine kalpas hence, she shall become a Buddha, titled Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, and Blessed One, named Free from Countless Hundreds of Thousands of Sufferings.
"By this, worthy one, you observe the conduct of a bodhisattva; whatever they practice is without fault and does not fall into states of transgression.
Then, the Bodhisattva Repeatedly Victorious King descended from the void, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One:

"A bodhisattva should practice skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and abide in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). If they exhort even a single person and guide them by means of the fundamental Dharma, they should immediately attain faith in skillful means through that very act. Even if they should fall into the great hells for as long as a hundred kalpas and encounter the most intense suffering and afflictions, they must endure them; rather, they would prefer to transform a single person so that they may establish the roots of virtue, without avoiding such hardships."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent! You have attained thorough penetration, O noble being; this is the practice of a bodhisattva’s great compassion, which transcends and delivers one from all sensations."
The Buddha said, "Son of good family!

I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a seeker named Jyotirasa who dwelt in forest thickets practicing auspicious vows. For four million two hundred thousand years he purely cultivated the Brahma-faring; when those years had passed, he entered the kingdom of Śāketa."
There was a potter’s daughter who, seeing that this student’s appearance was beautiful, handsome, and peerlessly exquisite, felt a profound surge of desire and immediately offered herself to him.
The student asked his sister, "What do you seek?"
He replied, "I admire benevolence.
Xuezhi said in response:
"I do not delight in desire.
The woman said,
"If it is not so, I shall take my own life."
Jyotīrasa thought to himself:
"I have guarded the prohibitions and purely cultivated the Brahma-faring for four million two hundred thousand years; if I were to now violate them, it would not be auspicious."
Having thought this, he set her aside; after walking seven paces away from her, he gave rise to compassion and said:

"If one violates the prohibitive precepts, they fall into hell. Rather than allowing this woman to harm herself in such a way, I would prefer that she attain peace and security, even if I must endure the agonies of hell."
Yan Guang immediately returned, took him by the arm again, and exhorted him, saying:
"Follow your own desires; do not bring peril upon yourself.

Xue Zhi withdrew from public life and devoted himself to his family's ancestral occupation for twelve years. Becoming weary of worldly constraints and practicing contentment, he purified the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). After his life ended, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!
If you wish to know who that bodhisattva Jvālāprabha was at that time, could he have been anyone other than [yourself]?"
"Do not form this view; it is I myself who am she.
The potter’s daughter was Gopī.
She pursued the desires of her heart for the sake of beauty, whereas I, out of great compassion, have transcended the hundreds of thousands of afflictions of birth and death."
"Wise one, observe this: while others who have committed offenses fall into the hells, the bodhisattva of skillful means ascends further to the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha told Hui-shang:
"If Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana had practiced skillful means, they would not have caused the bhikṣu Ghoṣila to fall into hell."

Why is this? I recall that in the past, during the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, there was a bhikṣu named Vimala who dwelt in a mountain cave in a secluded place. Not far from there were five ṛṣis. One day, a woman encountered a heavy rain on her way and hurried to take refuge in the cave where the bhikṣu Vimala resided; she departed once the rain had cleared.
When the five sages saw the woman, they each said, "This bhikṣu is lewd and impure; we call him unclean.
Vimalā, knowing the thoughts of the various seers, immediately leaped into the air, rising four *zhang* and nine *chi* above the ground.
When the various seers saw him flying through the air, they each said:
"According to what is recorded in our scriptures, one who is defiled by the dust of desire cannot fly."
Immediately, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and bowed his head in submission.
Had the bhikṣu not manifested these supernatural transformations, those five rishis would have fallen into the great hells.
At that time, the Bhikṣu Vimala was none other than the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
If Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana possessed the power of miraculous flight, then Gopikā would have had no way to fall into ruin.

One should know that this meaning cannot be fathomed by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; it is only the Bodhisattva who discerns and thoroughly understands skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). It is like a wanton woman who adorns herself in four ways and covets wealth and desire, or like a foolish person who alters human nature to make others follow their will by feigning the gift of their own body; they show respect to such a person until their resources are exhausted, and then they abandon them at a distance. Because of what she has gained, she feels no regret; the Bodhisattva of skillful means is also like this.

Observing the faculties of sentient beings who can be transformed, he employs whatever skillful means are necessary to guide and establish them; he reverently bestows himself upon sentient beings without begrudging his own body, planting the roots of all virtues without concealing or hiding his true intentions.

Suppose there is a person who has already established the roots of virtue; for the sake of such a person, one prolongs their life and increases their goodness. They harbor no longing or attachment toward any sensual pleasures, and they relinquish affection and love so that it returns to non-existence. Their mind is pure and free from all fetters, just as a honeybee gathers nectar from various flowers without forming the notion of permanence, causing not the slightest damage to the flowers' branches or leaves.

The Bodhisattva who practices skillful means follows worldly conventions and may enjoy various desires; yet he does not harbor attachment to those desires nor give rise to the notion of permanence. He neither destroys his own body nor harms others. This is like a seed that does not lose its fresh color, yet from it a sprout is born without any external addition or alteration.
Thus it is, son of good family!

By means of the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and through the vast wisdom of the perfection of knowledge (prajñāpāramitā), the bodhisattva enters into all worldly afflictions and acts according to whatever is desired; yet he does not abandon conventional practice, nor does he allow his body to become defiled by desire, nor does he contradict the Buddha’s praise, nor has he ever regressed.

Just as a fisherman draws in his line and spreads his net, acting according to his will to cut across the great currents and gathering in his lines and nets to obtain a great catch, so it is with the Bodhisattva.

Entering the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he abides in all wisdom with a subtle mind; bound by the great desire for the mind of universal supernormal wisdom, and through a mind free from grasping, he gains mastery over what he obtains and is born in the Brahma Heaven.
It is like a man skilled in the study of incantations who is captured by officials and bound with fivefold fetters.
If that man exercises his own will, he can sever all those bonds with a single incantation and escape.
In this way, son of good family!

A bodhisattva of skillful means enjoys the five desires for himself and shares them universally with the multitude; according to his pleasure, by the power of his wisdom and the power of his arts, he destroys all desires through a single supernormal knowledge and is reborn in the Brahma Heaven.

It is like a guide who, with a single-minded focus free from malice or aversion, manifests his power to provide shelter and escort a great merchant. Yet some may foolishly slander him, disparaging him by saying:
"If one examines this guide, even his own family and wealth do not conform to propriety; how could he possibly deliver the multitude and enable them to escape the bandits?"
‘I shall surely lose immeasurable wealth and treasures.

Thereupon, the guide was stirred with indignation and felt ashamed; he rose from his seat with a firm resolve, donned his armor, brandished his sword, and struck down his enemies, protecting [the caravan] in safety so that nothing was lost.

The Bodhisattva who practices skillful means wields the sword of wisdom according to the needs of the time; through clever expedients, he familiarizes himself with the five pleasures, even though these are not what those of the Disciple Vehicle (śrāvakayāna) find agreeable, thereby giving rise to compassion for them.
How can this be? If one indulges in heedless conduct, one cannot even save oneself; how then could one deliver the masses or subdue the demonic enemies?
Such a person is incapable of accompanying [the path].

By means of the dharma of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom and through skillful means at will, he uses the sword of wisdom to sever worldly afflictions and tear asunder the various nets; he wanders freely and at ease throughout all Buddha-lands, departing from lands of women that are free from defilement.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Priyadarśana who entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms in regular succession.

He arrived at the house of a noble family; that nobleman had a daughter named Śrīmatī who, while atop a multi-storied pavilion, heard the voice of the bhikṣu. As she went out to receive his food, she beheld his form and her mind became dissolute. Her desire was so intense that she could not fulfill her wish; her breath ceased and she passed away, her body trembling.
When a bhikṣu saw a woman and gave rise to impure thoughts, he immediately formed this thought:
"What is called the joy of the Dharma that one delights in?
When reckoned, it is empty and without reality, like water in a mirage; there is nothing therein to rely upon."
The ears, eyes, nose, mouth, body, and mind are like a lump of putrid flesh wrapped in leather and covered with skin; from the feet to the crown of the head, what is there to find delight in?

Contemplating the absence of contention and dispute, there is no ideation and no thought; dharmas have neither interior nor exterior, nor do they possess a life-span. Since nothing at all exists, what could the mind be attached to, and what could it receive?
"Permanently free from the blemish of desire, there is also no attainment.

When he contemplated all dharmas as being without arising, the Bodhisattva Aijing immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thereupon, filled with joy and exultation, he rose into the air at a height of four *zhang* and nine *chi* above the ground and circled the city of Śrāvastī seven times.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing the Bodhisattva Aigarjita (Love-Respect) ascending into the void like a king of geese, his supernormal powers unimpeded and acting with sovereign ease,
addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Do you see how Aigarjita soars and moves about like a king of geese?"
He replied, “I have seen it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“The Bodhisattva Aijing attained all Buddha-dharmas through the practice of desire for form; having subdued the demonic armies, he turned the Wheel of Dharma.

The maiden Zhixiang ultimately transformed her female body and was reborn in the Purple-Green Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where there spontaneously appeared a palace four hundred and eighty li in size, attended by fourteen thousand jade maidens.”
Relying on this merit, he gave rise to a mind of wisdom and thought to himself:
"By what practice was this birth attained?

He immediately knew that it originated from his former life in Śrāvastī as a daughter of a noble family, who had been deluded by and fondly attached to beauty. Due to these desires for sensual pleasure, at the end of her life she transformed from a woman into a man, spontaneously undergoing a divine transformation before a countless multitude.

"If even those whose minds are intent on sensual attachments obtain such a reward, how much more so for one with a pure and reverent heart who makes offerings and serves the Bodhisattva with the utmost respect?
'The pleasures of music and dance cannot last forever; we should go to the World-Honored One and visit the Bodhisattva whom we love and revere.'"

Thereupon, the devaputra and his retinue each took celestial flowers, sandalwood, and various incenses; with majestic and towering radiance, they all approached the World-Honored One and the Great Being Maitreya. They presented these flowers and incense as offerings, prostrated themselves before him, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and stood to one side. With palms joined, they praised him in verse:
“The Buddhas have no discursive thought, Their bliss is most immeasurable;
The Tathāgata has no mind or will, And thus attains the supreme path.”
"In Śrāvastī, I was a woman of inconceivable great fame and virtue, known as the daughter of the householder Ghoṣila;
beautiful and lovely, my body adorned with jewels, I was cherished by my parents.
There, the Son of the Perfectly Awakened One, who is free from attachment—"
His name is Greatness of Loving Reverence and Majestic Spirit.
Hearing his voice, soft and wondrous, my heart was filled with joy as I took the food and immediately proceeded to the Infinite Dharma.
Having seen him, my mind became disturbed; deluded by craving and desire, I was overcome by negligence.
Even if I cannot have my wish fulfilled, I shall simply reach the end of my life—what is the use of living on?
At that time, I could not utter a word; though I was offered food and drink, I could not accept it.
Because of my indulgence in sensual desire and negligence, I passed away right there.
Although he could not yet correspond to the practice of the Path, by casting off this blemished and defiled female body,
he attained the state of a male praised by the Buddha and was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The palace was most honored, subtle, and exquisite, composed of jewels beyond compare;
it had fourteen thousand retinues, with all the pleasures of court ladies fully provided.
Immediately, a thought arose spontaneously in his mind: "By what causes and conditions have I come to this?
He then recollected such matters as these: that the retribution for a heart of craving and desire is indeed thus.
Seeing him with a heart of love and reverence, one rejoices; yet with a mind of negligence, one gazes greedily.
By virtue of these causes, such is the retribution obtained, like the radiance illuminating a beautiful tree.
One who becomes a son or disciple of the Perfectly Awakened Buddha dwells wherever they may go in joy, securely established in wisdom;
such is the karmic reward for a mind of love and desire, let alone for one who makes offerings.
I am now truly a son of the Tathāgata; I vow to seek the sublime wisdom of the Buddha.
I shall practice for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Never abandoning my great resolve and nature.
All this is due to the kindness and respect shown by my virtuous teacher; Therefore, I shall make offerings to the Dharma and serve it.
Serving the Way without kin, one should only aspire to seek the path of awakening.
By practicing the conduct of the sublime and honored Way, even if one is attached to what is perceived with a heedless mind,
at that very moment one shall transform from a female body and immediately obtain the form of a courageous man.
The parents at home all wailed and wept; smelling the corpse lying on the ground, they tore at their hair and beat their breasts.
In their hearts they thought, "This is sorcery," and they cursed the śramaṇa with foul-mouthed abuse.
At that moment, the Devaputra, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, went to his parents and explained it all:
“Do not revile or become angry with the śramaṇa; lest you suffer affliction for a long night.”
"Do you wish to know whether I am here or not?
I have already leaped up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; at that moment, I transformed from a woman's body and became a celestial son of majestic radiance."
When one's parents arrive at the place of peace and security, yet first revile them with curses, one must personally repent of these transgressions;
though one seeks further protection, it cannot be found, for only the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom of the Path.
At that time, hearing the Buddha’s voice, their parents were courageously exhorted and converted;
with harmonious minds and liberated hearts, they went together with their retinues at once to the Buddha Śākyamuni.
There they bowed their heads together before the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, immediately repenting of their own angry and resentful thoughts.
All together they paid homage to the Tathāgata, inquiring about his well-being so that he might provide definitive clarification:
"By what offerings should one serve the Buddha?
What is meant by being in accord with the Dharma, the Buddha, and the Saṅgha?"
"Please explain this for our sake through your discernment.
If those who hear it have no distracted thoughts, the Most Victorious One will know what they intend.
Those who wish to make offerings to all Buddhas shall firm their resolve for the Way and master all mental conceptions.
His parents, kinsmen, and male and female attendants— five hundred in all, without omission—
hearing the discourse of the Great Being, simultaneously gave rise to the mind of the Great Way.
What the Most Victorious One has spoken is without deviation; Ānanda, listen to my words:
as the conduct of a Bodhisattva is boundless, they abide in wisdom through skillful means;
may my love and reverence for the Bodhisattvas be thus.
"If a woman loves and respects me, I shall cause her to transform her female form, quickly becoming a man, the most excellent among men.

Ānanda, observe this power of my name and virtue: whereas others fall into hell because of their indulgent minds and craving for sensual forms, she has been transformed into a man through her love and desire."
The Devaputra Cittamati made offerings to me, Always attaining abundant peace through his reverence;
Having made those offerings for incalculable eons, He shall become a Buddha named Sarvadarśin.
These five hundred people have resolved their minds on the Way; they too shall personally attain the state of the Honored One among Men.
Who, upon hearing this, would not make offerings to the Buddha? Their hearts will be filled with immeasurable joy and peace.
Calculating those who love and revere this bodhisattva, the women he has transformed and enlightened are not merely one or two;
they number immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas. By establishing them on the Way through their hearts of desire, he becomes the Greatly Virtuous One named Bhaiṣajyarāja.
"For what reason would a bodhisattva have impurity?
Because they bestow peace and security even upon those who cause affliction through the dust of worldly toil—how much more so for those who offer worship and service?
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is just as when someone approaches Mount Sumeru; they all become golden in color, following the light that illuminates the mountain.

Likewise, if one harbors a heart of joy and a desire for the meaningful, or a mind dedicated to the Dharma, and succeeds in drawing near to a Bodhisattva, one will attain a uniform state. One’s nature will naturally incline toward the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*). From this day forward, I shall serve the Bodhisattva like Mount Sumeru, or like a king of medicines called 'Seeing Cures' (*Dṛṣṭisādhaka*): whether one possesses a pure mind or a mind of anger, upon seeing this medicine, all ailments are eliminated. In the same way, whether the mind is pure or impure, or if it is a mind of lust, anger, and delusion, those who behold the Bodhisattva will have them all cured."
Then the Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent, Ānanda!
It is truly as you have said."
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are inconceivable; wherever they travel, they manifest for the sake of all sentient beings the desire for fearlessness—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas practice only this dharma, whereas bodhisattvas universally protect them, causing them to further enter the tracks of all-encompassing wisdom. Using skillful means, they comply with their inclinations, never feeling revulsion toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"May I offer a parable to praise the conduct of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas?
The Buddha said:
"How lamentable! Kāśyapa said:
"Suppose there were a vast wilderness, desolate and devoid of people, where a wall had spontaneously arisen reaching as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, with only a single gate."
Countless people all entered the wilderness; not far from there was a great city where the land was fertile and rice and grain were extremely cheap. Its happiness is beyond words;
the population was so vast it could not be calculated, and those within that city were as steadfast as adamant.

Beside the city there is a river, and along the riverbank there is a road. In the midst of this desolate road there was a wise man, intelligent and mindful of the meaning [of the path], who felt compassion for those entering the wilderness and desired to deliver them. Raising his voice, he made this solemn declaration:
"The great city of peace, where there is forever no fear of death, is not far from this wilderness; I am your guide, come to lead you toward that which you desire."
The multitude replied, "We shall not go;
remaining here without moving, we wish to see the image of the city appear spontaneously, and only then will we depart."
At that time, there were others who understood the subtle meaning, and they replied:
"We shall go, following wherever you, O Benevolent One, may lead.
We are people of such meager merit that having heard this voice, we did not believe it nor find joy in it; we did not follow its teaching and thus did not cross the wilderness."
That subtle person then crossed the wilderness; observing the path by the river, he mounted it and proceeded forward.
On both sides of the path lay deep, vast ravines hundreds of thousands of feet deep, covered with various grasses and trees.
If bridges are built in the four directions, one will cross the perilous paths without obstruction;
even if great bandits pursue from behind, there is no fear, for the bandits will naturally retreat and never look back again.
Advancing step by step, he was neither afraid nor terrified; without looking left or right, he beheld a great city.
As he drew closer to the city walls, his mind was free from doubt; entering that city, he manifested his majestic deportment for immeasurable people, increasing their merit and fortune.
After Kāśyapa had finished his praise, he offered this analogy:
"The vast wilderness refers to the perils of saṃsāra.
The wall reaching as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three refers to the sensual desires of affection to which the unwise become attached."
"There is but one gate" refers to the Mahāyāna.
"People entering a vast wilderness" refers to the ignorant and deluded ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
"A clever person making a vow to call out to the multitude" refers to the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s joy in the practice of *apramāṇa* (the immeasurables) for the sake of delivering others.
Those of inferior resolve who do not proceed but wish to see the city refer to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
One should say to them:
"You shall go; follow wherever you intend to head."
This refers to the Bodhisattva.
Those who hear the sound and do not believe refer to the various heterodox paths and erroneous practices of non-Buddhist schools.
"Crossing the wilderness" refers to upholding diligence to reach all-encompassing wisdom and cultivating the various samādhis.
The road passing through the river refers to the Dharma-gates.
The great mountain stream of hundreds of thousands of zhang to the left refers to the stage of the Śrāvakas.
The great mountain stream of hundreds of thousands of zhang to the right refers to the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
The great arrangement of grasses and woods to construct bridges in the four directions refers to the perfection of wisdom through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
The unimpededness in proceeding in the four directions refers to the Bodhisattva’s practice of the four ways of attracting beings (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) to gather immeasurable people.
That the pursuers do not dare to fear and naturally retreat refers to the retinues of Māra and all those who practice dependent conduct.
That one never looks back refers to the Perfection of Patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Advancing step by step, he considers himself transformed and enlightened by the Bodhisattva; this is the Perfection of Vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
Furthermore, his lack of fear means that he arouses the resolve of sentient beings with a pure mind; this is the Perfect Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
"Not looking to the left or right" means not setting one's heart on the benefits of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"Then seeing the great city" means attaining all-encompassing wisdom and supernatural powers.
To be "slightly near the city" means to practice the merit of the Path of Seeing and cultivate the Buddha-wisdom.
To have "no doubt in one's mind" means to understand wisdom, skillful means, and the various *pāramitās*; thus, one is able to universally observe all sentient beings without fear or aversion.
Having just entered the city, he is one who manifests rites for the benefit of immeasurable people to increase their merit and fortune; that is to say, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"When the Buddha, the God among Gods, has just arisen in the world, he establishes the Bodhisattvas in their titles and extensively builds up their benefit and meaning.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
He then sighed at this parable.
As these words were being spoken, twelve thousand devas and humans conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa:

"His virtuous conduct is beyond measure; his learning of the truths is subtle, and his skillful means are excellent. In all that a Great Being does, he does not act for his own sake nor bestow upon others; he speaks neither of a self nor of another."
Then the Bodhisattva Prajñottara addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What is meant by ‘one who is in his last birth’?

Yet at the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa, you spoke these words: ‘One must go to visit this shaven-headed śramaṇa; how could he possibly possess the Way? The Buddha-way is difficult to attain. For what reason did the World-Honored One speak thus on that occasion?”
The Buddha said to Hui-shang:
"Stop for a moment,
son of good family!"
One should not establish fixed limits regarding the level characteristics of the Tathāgatas and the practices of the bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva are inconceivable; any true person (*satpuruṣa*) should form this view that they are transformed beings (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*).
Listen, son of good family, and reflect upon this well.

There is a dharma called the Bodhisattva of Skillful Means (*upāya-kauśalya*); since the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the wisdom he has aroused has been inconceivable, and he dares to initiate and preach the Bodhisattva teachings as is appropriate for the times.

Since seeing the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, I have attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). I am without a single flaw or deficiency and have nothing forgotten; my mind is undisturbed and my wisdom is unimpaired. Having already attained this patience of dharmas, as a bodhisattva who has accomplished his task, I can attain Buddhahood in a single thought-moment, which is equivalent to seven days. For one with the aspiration for bodhi, the interval between the initial resolve and its fulfillment is likened to an entire kalpa.

To manifest everywhere for all people to enlighten and transform sentient beings, and by the power of wisdom to seek to attain the great, equal enlightenment of Buddhahood—praising and initiating [the cultivation of] immeasurable billions of kalpas against false views—is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Even if the various śrāvakas were to attain mastery in their practice, they would never possess such a samādhi as this; they do not reach the concentration of the bodhisattva’s samādhi, wherein the body remains unmoving and the mind is free from conceptualization—a state that is beyond the reach of the bodies and minds of ordinary people."

Furthermore, causing the Bodhisattva’s samādhi and right reception to neither advance nor retreat, constantly using the four means of attraction to rescue and gather all sentient beings, not losing diligence and not falling into indolence, while preaching the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) to the multitude—this is called the skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) of a Bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

At the very moment a bodhisattva resolves his mind [on enlightenment], he attains perfect true awakening in the Tuṣita Heaven and turns the wheel of Dharma. Although the people of Jambudvīpa cannot ascend to the Tuṣita Heaven to hear and receive the Dharma, the bodhisattva thinks: 'The various devas in heaven are able to descend here.'"
Therefore, O noble son, manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood in Jambudvīpa is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, O son of good family!
When a Bodhisattva resolves his mind, he is able to vanish suddenly from Tuṣita Heaven and, without passing through a womb, attain supreme perfect enlightenment in a single moment.
Those nearby may have doubts as to where he has come from, wondering: "Is this a deva?"
Is this the work of a Gandharva’s transformation?
If one harbors doubt and does not listen to or accept the Dharma, for this reason the Bodhisattva manifests dwelling within a womb; this is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Do not give rise to the thought:
'The Bodhisattva dwells within the womb.'"
"Do not harbor such thoughts; Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not arise from a womb of semen. Why is this?
There is a samādhi called 'Stainless,' and it is by means of this correct reception that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas adorn themselves."
The devas of Tuṣita say that when the Bodhisattva passes away from there, he does not waver; they do not see him entering a womb.

Yet he manifests dwelling within his mother’s belly and is born from her side; he abandons his kingdom and home, and immediately sits beneath the tree of enlightenment. He displays diligent ascetic practices, manifesting everywhere in all places without changing anything, remaining free from weariness and untainted by defilement.
"Why is this? Because the manifestations of a bodhisattva’s auspicious signs purify those who are transformed; this is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Hui-shang:
"Why does the Bodhisattva transform his own body into the color of purple-polished gold and manifest entry into the womb? Huisang replied:
"He is of a tranquil, pure, and luminous nature."
The World-Honored One said:

"It is so. That bodhisattva, standing above all sentient beings, is the most supreme; he has come through transformation, beyond the reach of gods and humans alike—this is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva."
"Why is it that when the Bodhisattva dwells in his mother’s womb, he remains there for a full ten months and is born without having seen anything?
If people were to conceive the thought that while in their mother’s embrace, the days and months are insufficient and the sense faculties are incomplete."
The manifestation of completing ten months is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva.
Why was the Bodhisattva born in a grove rather than in the inner palace?

Because for a long night the Bodhisattva has practiced dwelling in seclusion; his will delights in tranquility, and he practices pure equanimity. He desires that devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans shall all abandon their dwellings to offer silent worship. These various flowers and incenses shall flow throughout the world, causing the people of Kapilavastu to rejoice and be filled with gladness, so that they do not fall into negligence. For this reason, the Bodhisattva was born beneath a tree in a place of solitude, not within the palace halls; this is the skillful means of the Bodhisattva.
"Why was the Bodhisattva born from the right side?
If it were not so, people would harbor doubts, thinking that the Bodhisattva entered the womb through the union of semen and blood, rather than being born through miraculous transformation."
The multitude would surely harbor doubts and hesitations, finding it difficult to reach a resolution; therefore, he manifested this to enable people to attain understanding and liberation.

Although the Bodhisattva was born from the right side, his mother suffered no injury or pain from his entry or exit. This was because the noble sages of antiquity acted in such a manner according to the occasion, never deviating from what is appropriate; this is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why did the Bodhisattva’s mother grasp a tree branch before giving birth?
Had it not been so, people would have said:
'Although the Queen gave birth to the Bodhisattva, she must have suffered affliction and pain; she was no different from ordinary commoners.'"

Desiring to manifest peace and security for the common people, his mother happened to grasp a tree branch; as her disposition was gentle and mild, the Bodhisattva was born. This is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why is it that the Bodhisattva is born suddenly in such peaceful serenity, his body pure and free from all defilement?

The Bodhisattva is supreme, standing above the three realms; though dwelling within the womb, he is like the sun shining upon water—pure, unattached, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, he manifests birth from the side, unlike ordinary beings; this is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)."
"Why is it that as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, Śakra descended first to prostrate himself in homage and receive him, rather than any other deva?
It is because Śakra established this fundamental vow from time immemorial:
'If a Bodhisattva is born, I shall receive him with a pure mind.'"
This is also a sign of the fundamental virtue of a bodhisattva; it is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
For what reason did the Bodhisattva, immediately after being born, walk seven steps upon the ground and not eight?
This is the auspicious response of a true being (satpuruṣa), one who awakens to or awakens others to the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga).
From antiquity until the present, there has never been anyone able to manifest these seven steps; this is the skillful means (upāyakauśalya) of the Bodhisattva.
"Why is it that as soon as the Bodhisattva had taken seven steps, he raised his hand and said:
'In this world, including the heavens above and the earth below, I am the most supreme; I shall bring an end to the very source of birth, old age, and death!'"

At that time, the assembly was gathered without exception, including Śakra, Brahmā, brahmins, and all the sons of gods; had he not manifested himself there, each would have regarded themselves as superior, harboring arrogance and thus no longer wishing to pay homage to or attend upon the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva takes pity on the non-Buddhist brahmins and the hosts of devas, who have been ill at ease for a long night and will surely fall into the evil realms to undergo suffering and pain.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva raises his voice and praises himself:

"In the world, I am the foremost among the World-Honored Ones, the supreme among the heavens and the earth; my skillful means and wisdom are transcendent and extraordinary, walking alone without peer, and I shall bring to an end the very roots of birth, old age, and death."
With this voice, he announced it throughout the trichiliocosm.
Those sons of gods who had not yet arrived came immediately upon hearing the sound.

At that time, the heterodox practitioners, brahmins, and all the sons of gods together bowed their heads in respectful salutation and praised the voice; with palms joined, they returned in sincere devotion. This is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why does the Bodhisattva smile with great joy, without harboring frivolity, and why does he smile without a sycophantic smile?
The Bodhisattva then gave rise to this thought:

"All classes of beings were originally one with me; yet, having resolved upon the supreme path and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, they fearfully succumb to indolence, negligence, and self-indulgence, thereby becoming base, ignorant, and arrogant."
"Or, by means of sound and voice, they understand all dharmas; through their diligence and swift penetration toward all supernormal wisdoms, they cause beings to take refuge in the Buddha.

With such great compassion, they rouse sentient beings and eliminate their negligence; having seen them, they vow that those beings shall also universally possess the fruits [of practice]. For this reason, the Righteous One manifests a great joyful smile; this is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why does the Bodhisattva, who is pure and stainless, bathe again, being seen and served by Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings?
All ordinary people must bathe upon their first birth; the Bodhisattva, though pure, bathes in accordance with worldly custom."
How much more so for worldly people? Therefore, he manifests this meaning as the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
For what reason did the Bodhisattva, after his birth, go to a secluded place and sit beneath a tree before entering the city?

Desiring to fulfill the roots of all faculties, he manifests the pleasures of the inner palace—stringed songs, performances, and music—and lights four lamps; through these manifest conditions, he encourages the multitude to learn and exhort them to renounce wealth and treasures, delighting in ascending to the sublime. Entering the household and then departing from it again, he does not engage in heterodox practices; leaving home to study the Way, he sits beneath the Bodhi tree. This is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
"Why did the Bodhisattva’s mother pass away seven days after his birth?
Her lifespan having reached its end, her merit should have caused her to ascend to heaven; it was not the Bodhisattva’s fault.

While previously dwelling in Tuṣita, he observed that Queen Māyā’s life was about to end, with only ten months and seven days remaining. Therefore, through a supernatural transformation, he descended from Tuṣita and manifested entry into the Queen’s womb. Judging by this, it was not the Bodhisattva’s fault; rather, it was the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)."
"Why does a bodhisattva study writing, archery, horsemanship, weaponry, arts, and crafts, as well as games such as *chuppo*?

It is to conform to worldly customs according to present causes and conditions; to demonstrate that they have studied all the musical performances found throughout the trichiliocosm, the essential doctrines of the sūtras, poetry, incantations, medical treatments, and even jesting and satire, becoming universally learned in everything without exception. This is intended to prevent commoners from becoming arrogant, and this constitutes the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva."
