The Sūtra of the Great Skillful Means as Questioned by Bodhisattva Prajñottara, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
"Why does the Bodhisattva take a wife? The Bodhisattva is free from desire and does not prize a mate;
in his state of detachment, he is a true gentleman. Yet, because he manifests a retinue, a wife, and children, bystanders harbor doubts, wondering:
'Is the Bodhisattva not a man, but rather a eunuch?'"
Desiring to eliminate their lingering doubts, he took Gopī, the daughter of the Śākyas, as his wife; it was on this account that he manifested the birth of a son, Rāhula.
To argue that Rāhula was born from a womb is not, in truth, the correct meaning.

Why is this so? Rāhula has passed away from the celestial realm to be born by transformation; he was not raised through the union of parents, but rather as the result of the original vows of a bodhisattva.
In the past, under Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Gopī made a vow:
"In a future age, I shall become your wife and plant the roots of virtue.

Because he did not violate this long-standing agreement, he took her as his wife. Yet, while worldly people are agitated by their lack of focus, becoming deluded by sensual desires and clinging to them with fervor, the Bodhisattva manifested a wife, children, and kinsmen, only to subsequently renounce his kingdom.
Some may say: "If even the consort of a True Being (sadbhūta), who was so upright, beautiful, and exquisite, could still renounce her, how much more so should we?
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva first began his study of the Way, all his wives, retinues, and kinsmen, out of mutual respect and esteem, made this vow together:
"Life after life we shall be with you, O Benevolent One; in birth after birth we shall serve you, following you until you attain the Way of the Buddha.

Thus he extensively expounded the pure and white Dharma, whereby forty-two thousand ladies of the inner palace resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true Way, while all other classes of beings were delivered from the evil realms. For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests having a retinue.

As for those palace ladies who were afflicted by the passions of love and affection, upon seeing the Bodhisattva—serene, pure, and like a bright moon-pearl—they immediately became free from carnal desire.
Suppose a bodhisattva were to manifest a transformation being whose facial features and appearance were identical to his own.
At that time, the court ladies would engage with this transformed person in all manner of pleasures, each thinking to herself:
"Today we are together with the Bodhisattva, yet our aspirations and inclinations are forever different."
At that time, the Bodhisattva went beneath the shade of a Jambu tree and sat in meditative concentration; he dwelt in joyful tranquility, like a transformation produced by a magical being.

Since the Bodhisattva first followed Dīpaṃkara Buddha, all that he has seen regarding the karma of the causes and conditions of desire and passion is the responsive manifestation of influences from time immemorial; this constitutes the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why did the Bodhisattva sit in meditative contemplation under the shade of the Jambu tree and transform seven billion devaputras, causing them to resolve upon the path?
Furthermore, he desired that the Queen see him and think to herself:
'I must surely leave the household life.'"
"For this reason, the Bodhisattva sat in the shade of the Jambu tree and meditated in stillness; this was the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Why did the Bodhisattva leave home at midnight and go to the river to bathe himself?"
To inspire all living beings, he manifests the roots of virtue, causing them all to reflect:
"The merit established in this place is spontaneous, for it is the nature of the pure and white Dharma.

Thus, departing from home at midnight without hindrance, one must utterly renounce all matters of worldly pleasure; yet the pure and white Dharma must not be abandoned. This is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a Bodhisattva.

"Why is it that while the Bodhisattva was exhorting and transforming the devas in the Tuṣita Heaven, they beseeched him with palms joined, saying, 'The time has come; you may now depart,' and the gates opened spontaneously as he descended to manifest his birth?"
The Bodhisattva thought:
"If the King should harbor doubts and fail to understand this upon hearing it, he will remain unsettled for a long night; encountering fear and affliction, he may fall into the evil realms."
Therefore, he manifested as a celestial being; the celestial being opened the door, and from within the assembly, the various devas raised their voices in praise.
This was not the fault of the Bodhisattva; wishing to comfort the king’s heart, he attributed it to the gods.
Observing this meaning, one provides exhortation and transformation; this is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
For what reason does the bodhisattva abandon his kingdom and renounce kingship, appearing to depart?

People should understand that it is out of fear of birth, old age, sickness, and death that a bodhisattva leaves the household life; it is not for the sake of increasing or avoiding the company of family, kin, relatives, or associates. This is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
"Why does the Bodhisattva shave his own head and beard?

Among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, and non-humans throughout the trichiliocosm, none are able to even behold the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head, much less be worthy of shaving his hair and beard."
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having exhorted and delivered sentient beings, shaved off his own hair and beard. King Śuddhodana thought with resentment:
"Who has shaved my son's head?
Upon hearing from the messengers, he learned that the Bodhisattva had shaved it himself.
The King then remained silent; this was the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
For what reason did the Bodhisattva take the precious necklace, crown, and turban, hand them over to Chandaka, and stir up various thoughts?
The Bodhisattva, for the sake of the Way, no longer craves the pleasure of precious ornaments; he has no attachment to any thing and therefore relinquishes them all.
In future generations, those in the borderlands shall take the Bodhisattva as their model:

"We who have left the household life should likewise study this; following the Buddha-dharma, we rely upon the four noble practices and remain unattached to all things, not leaving the home life out of doubt regarding the aggregates (skandhas) or the sense bases (āyatanas)."
"If it were not so, people would suspect him and say:
'He has left the household life because he does not know how to manage a livelihood!
This is the skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) of a bodhisattva."
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family! Listen now."
For what reason did this Bodhisattva resolve to practice asceticism for six years?

It was because there were karmic transgressions among the various Bodhisattvas; thus he manifested diligent suffering as a provisional skillful means for the sake of all sentient beings, which is the purpose of this Bodhisattva’s undertaking.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he spoke these words:
"He is merely a shaven-headed śramaṇa; how can he be a Buddha?
This was the skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) of the Bodhisattva.
One should understand this meaning.
For what reason did the Bodhisattva speak these words?

Udumbara (translated in the Jin language as "Supreme Aspiration"), also known as Jyotīrasa ("Flame Flower"), had five close friends and five hundred disciples. Being a son of noble lineage from a great Brahmin family, he originally studied the Mahāyāna; however, he was led astray and deluded by evil associates, thereby losing his resolve for the Path.

Those five close friends believed in external heterodox teachings and did not follow the true doctrine; they practiced the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths and did not study the Buddha-dharma. Claiming themselves to possess the Way, they served as teachers for others, and they themselves declared, "We are Buddhas," and their five hundred disciples were likewise so.
The student Yanhua, entering among those of such inclinations through skillful means, spoke these words to rebuke Nandika:
"What is this so-called Buddha?
A shaven-headed śramaṇa! The path of the Buddha is difficult to attain; why go to visit him?"
Then, the Flower-of-Flame gradually transformed five sons of noble family and five hundred disciples who were followers of other teachings; therefore, he spoke these words:
"What is this that is called a Buddha?"
"Shaved-headed śramaṇas! The Buddha-way is difficult to attain.
The Buddha said to Hui-shang:

"Observe that in that world, the student Yantuhua was at that time standing upright in another place together with five close friends and a retinue of five hundred. At that moment, a potter named Nandika (in the Jin language, 'Joyful') went to his location and praised the merits of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa."
The scholar Jyotīrasa said,
"Come, let us go together to visit Kāśyapa Buddha.
Jyotīrasa thought to himself:

"These disciples have not yet fulfilled the roots of virtue that serve as the basis for their aspirations; if I were now to praise the merits of the Way of Tathāgata Kāśyapa and disparage those of other schools, these sons of noble family would surely stand stunned and would certainly not proceed together with me."

For this reason, Jyotīrasa protected his original vow with boundless wisdom; yet, by means of skillful expedients, he said: "The shaven-headed śramaṇas are not the Buddha; the Way of the Buddha is difficult to attain. Where does such boundless wisdom reside?"
"One who practices the Perfection of Wisdom has no notion of self or other, nor does he have a notion of the Path.
The Flower of Flame, having attained ultimate wisdom of emptiness and being universally unattached, follows all dharmas through skillful means; therefore, he spoke these words.

The scholar Yaṃpuṣpa, together with his five close friends and five hundred disciples, went to the side of a pond; having finished bathing and emerged from the water, he mounted a horse-drawn carriage along with his five close friends and his disciples, traveling about to preach the sutras.

At that time, Ānanda, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority and desiring to transform that teacher and his followers, went out to meet the one riding the flaming flower chariot along with his companions and disciples; he then exchanged greetings with them, asking from where they had come.
Huan-yü replied with sincerity,
"I have returned from an audience with Kāśyapa Buddha. Yan-hua said:
"The shaven-headed śramaṇas are not the Buddha; the Way of the Buddha is difficult to attain.
When the potter heard this, he was deeply displeased and seized [the man's] hair with his hand, saying:
"If you do not believe me, let us go together to question him."

Jyotīṣka reflected: "Huan-yü’s character is peaceful, stable, gentle, and harmonious; he has never been impulsive or violent. Even now that he is pressing me urgently, he will ultimately not forget [his nature]."
"I and my disciples ought to be companions, together observing his Way.
They all replied, "So be it."
Thereupon, the potter, Yamapushpa, and their five companions, along with five hundred disciples, went together to visit Kāśyapa Buddha.
The Buddha then expounded for them the fundamental roots of the moral conduct they had cultivated in previous lives.
Their hearts were filled with joy and exultation, and they praised Yaṣṭikā, saying:
"The World-Honored One’s virtue, wisdom, and skillful means are such as these; why did he not speak for us sooner?
When the disciples of the five friends saw Kāśyapa Buddha, his virtue was majestic and his eloquence immeasurable, and they all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa preached the karma of the Mahāyāna, expounding the treasury of the Dharma and the wheel of non-retrogression; the five great brahmins and their five hundred disciples all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Buddha told Hui-shang: "Noble son!
Listen."

If Yaṃpuṣpa had praised the Venerable Kāśyapa with the wisdom of a Buddha and disparaged those of other schools, the five great brahmins and their five hundred disciples would never have been converted.
Furthermore, there would have been no way for them to behold Kāśyapa Buddha. Because he wished to transform them, he employed skillful means and spoke these words:
"The shaven-headed śramaṇa is not the Buddha; the Way of the Buddha is difficult to attain."
"Having attained non-retrogression, there is nothing they do not penetrate and they no longer doubt the Way; this is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Huishang:

"The reason a bodhisattva manifests according to the times like a transformation (*nirmāṇa*), appearing to undergo the practice of remaining under affliction and hardship, is that if it were otherwise, the śramaṇas and brahmins who purely observe the precepts, as well as the common people, would fail to recognize [the truth], becoming indolent and failing to progress."
Having just met, they have attained this treasury of non-discourse and this treasury of difference.

Throughout the long night, these beings have never possessed beneficial meaning; failing to attain peace and stability, they return to the evil realms due to their many transgressions. It is for this reason that the Tathāgata manifests that his remaining karmic retribution is not yet exhausted.

Bodhisattvas are entirely free from the affliction of the hindrances of transgression. When śramaṇas or brahmins who uphold the precepts utter coarse words, they should immediately feel self-doubt, thinking: "If I do not apply diligent effort, I shall not attain liberation. To those who harbor such hesitant intentions, the Bodhisattva uses skillful means to speak these words:

"By this means you shall deliver them; you should then say of yourselves: 'We were ignorant and have now reproached ourselves for our errors and repented. We shall only study the wisdom of the Path and practice universal reverence."

Furthermore, because the heterodox teachers of the outside were arrogant and self-indulgent, the Tathāgata practiced austerities for six years; this was not on account of any remaining karmic retribution. Why is this so?

There were certain śramaṇas and brahmins who, while maintaining purity and self-mastery, subsisted on only one sesame seed and one grain of rice. Desiring to encompass such individuals and fulfill their aspirations, the Bodhisattva limited his daily intake to one sesame seed and one grain of rice. Had he not eaten at these times, he would have been unable to return to the Noble Path.
The Bodhisattva spoke these words:
"The shaven-headed śramaṇa cannot be the Buddha; the Way of the Buddha is difficult to attain.
Thus, he incurred the karmic retribution of practicing asceticism for six years. That which was opened and delivered during those six years is beyond the comprehension of those of other schools.

Furthermore, causing five million two hundred thousand followers of external paths to abide in the wisdom of equality, and being able to manifest and transform the people he encounters—this is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why has the Tathāgata gathered the fourfold assembly—devas, nāgas, spirits, and humans and non-humans—to preach this sutra?
As the first watch of the night was ending, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Bring me my middle robe; my body feels slightly cold."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately took it and presented it to him.
When the first watch of the night had ended and the middle watch began, he again commanded Ānanda to bring his upper robe, saying:
"I am cold and wish to put it on."
He then proceeded further.
When the middle watch of the night had ended and the final watch had begun, he again commanded Ānanda:
"Bring the robe for the assembly; I wish to wear it."
He then stepped forward again.
The Buddha put on the robes and addressed the bhikṣus:
“I permit those who have left home to study to wear the three dharma-robes at once; even if it is cold, they may layer them.”

Why is this? In future generations, there will be frontier regions and cold, chilly kingdoms and cities where single-layered garments will not suffice; according to the local conditions, one must wear double layers.
The Buddha has neither cold nor heat, neither hunger nor thirst.

Why is this? Because if one dwells in a cold land and does not wear double-layered robes, one may fall ill, or become weary and retreat, and thus be unable to fulfill the intention of seeking the Way to its ultimate end; this is the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why does the Tathāgata sit upon a mat of grass?

It is for the sake of those who will become renunciants and students in future generations, lest they become attached to fine and beautiful beds, seats, couches, and desks, and fail to apply diligent effort because their minds are set on comfort and softness; or lest those with little merit, unable to obtain fine seats, woolen rugs, carpets, layered mats, quilts, or bedding, should harbor resentment and retreat."
One should reflect in one's mind, saying:
"When the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, was about to attain Buddhahood, he sat upon a mat of grass; he did not rely on a fine couch, yet he attained the Way of the Buddha."
"How much less, then, should we covet fine seats?

The Buddha said, "As for my teachings, they follow local customs; whether one uses heavy carpets or layered mats, it does not hinder the Way. One should find no pleasure in the fine and soft, nor feel distress over the coarse and hard, for human minds are difficult to harmonize and their dispositions and practices vary."
Therefore, he manifests various teachings through skillful adaptation; this is the Tathāgata’s excellent skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"For what reason does a bodhisattva again arise to eat and drink, rather than seeking the Way by fasting while remaining among those without virtue?"
Since one who is hungry cannot give rise to wisdom, it is through the cause of eating with peace and security that one accomplishes the Way and its virtue.

When preaching the Dharma of the Bodhisattva to transform all sentient beings, he brings about much peace and security without toil or hardship; the Bodhisattva receives food and is thereby able to attain Buddhahood. From this, he reaches a single samādhi, abiding in that one samādhi for hundreds of thousands of kalpas—this is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva.
"Why does the Bodhisattva dwell in seclusion seeking the Way?

He spreads a mat of grass beneath a tree, following the example of past Buddhas who did not covet couches or seats. Seated upon this spread, he preaches the Truths, auspiciousness, and the principles of propriety. Should the Bodhisattva preach the Dharma in brief, it enters into beneficial meaning. Any who offer grass to the Bodhisattva thereby give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. At that time, the Buddha bestows upon them the prophecy of auspiciousness:
'In the future, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Vimala Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.'"
This is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
For what reason does the bodhisattva cause the hosts of Māra to assemble beneath the Bodhi tree?
If he were not to swiftly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, that Māra Pāpīyān would not dare to approach the bodhisattva’s dwelling.
Furthermore, son of good family!
When the Bodhisattva first sat beneath the tree, he thought to himself:
"Who is the most venerable among the four realms of the desire world?"
"Those among men who follow my teaching, I shall cause to come before me so that we may engage in battle and settle this once and for all.
At that time, because he had fully entered into all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms, he caused Māra to put him to the test.

Of Māra’s eighty-four thousand *koṭis* of troops—consisting of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—all gave rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; this was the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why has the Tathāgata, having already attained the Way of the Buddha, remained seated for seven days without rising, observing the tree without weariness?
These sons of the gods, moved by the transformation of his virtuous conduct, were filled with great joy and each thought to themselves:
'We should seek to know upon what this Tathāgata’s mind relies.'"
For seven consecutive nights, he focused his mind with single-minded diligence, yet he could not find it.

Because of this, he beheld the thirty-two marks of the World-Honored One; his heart leaped with joy, and he resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, vowing that in a future age he too would attain such a state and sit beneath the Bodhi tree.
For this reason, the Tathāgata sat beneath the tree for seven days; this constitutes the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Why is it that after the Bodhisattva has attained Buddhahood, he exhorts and leads the countless multitudes of devas and humans?
Brahmā did not request it, nor did he preach the Dharma; thereupon, the Tathāgata thought to himself:

"There is an incalculable assembly of devas in the desire realm, along with the retinues of Māra, ghosts, spirits, and rākṣasas. If they were to see the Bodhisattva’s lion’s roar and his strides, they would immediately give rise to the aspiration for the Way; those who see him with joy will, by that condition, attain the unconditioned."
"Furthermore, son of noble family!
When the Bodhisattva goes beneath the tree of enlightenment, he immediately emits light from the mark on his crown (uṣṇīṣa), which universally illuminates the palaces of Māra and the trichiliocosm.

From within that radiance, a single voice proclaims: 'Now the Honored One, the Son of the Śākya clan, the Able One (Śākyamuni), has abandoned his kingdom and renounced his home; he has now perfected the path of Unsurpassed, Right, and True Enlightenment. Having already passed beyond your realm, he has delivered many people in numbers beyond measure, leaving your domain empty. You should go forth at once to engage him in battle.'"
When Māra heard this, he was filled with great sorrow and distress; he arrayed his fourfold army, numbering thirty nayuta-koti-bhūta in total, and went to the Bodhi tree.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, by means of the jewel of wisdom, established his great arm of compassionate and luminous insight—superb like purple-polished gold—and was revered by the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, Śakra, and Brahmā.
At that time, the brahmin thought:
"Brahmā has transformed me; I am born from Brahmā, and none can surpass me.
There is no venerable teacher in the world greater than Brahmā."
The Tathāgata thought to himself:

"I shall cause Brahmā to appear so that all people may see him; for the devas, nāgas, and spirits all rely upon Brahmā. Since even Brahmā bows his head in prostration to the Buddha, it is fitting that he should provide encouragement and assistance as I preach the Dharma accordingly; if there were no such request, the Tathāgata would not speak."

"Relying on the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, I shall cause Brahmā to come and assist with exhortation through the Dharma; if all people should reverently keep Brahmā in mind, they shall likewise exhort the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, Brahmā departed from his own palace and came to the World-Honored One.

When Mahābrahmā exhorted the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, six million eight hundred thousand Brahmās all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and they all praised him in verse, saying:
“The Buddha’s honor is without limit; He is most supreme and unattainable.
Practicing skillful means and expedients— This is what makes one a Tathāgata.”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Hui-shang:
"The remaining karmic retributions manifested by the Tathāgata are ten in number; these too are the World-Honored One’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

You should understand that they are [the result of] his utmost sincerity. If one wished to cause the Tathāgata to have even a hair’s breadth of flaw, or to be incomplete in planting the roots of virtue, or to have shortcomings such that his conduct were not fully perfected—yet he has attained perfect enlightenment and sat beneath the Bodhi tree—this is simply not the case."
Why is this? Because he has fully realized the pure and white dharmas, free from all blemishes.
O son of noble family!
If you wish to know, the Tathāgata has already cast off all unwholesome dharmas.
The World-Honored One is unimpeded; how much less would he maintain defilement or have any remaining karmic retribution?

The Buddha is the King of Physicians, who eliminates all illnesses and possesses no obscurations (āvaraṇa); yet, for the sake of blessing sentient beings, he manifests the appearance of remaining faults.

It is because he wishes to cause the multitude to protect their body, speech, and mind, and to cultivate pure conduct. It is like a son of a noble and distinguished clan who has grown up in the royal household and been accustomed to milk and curd; yet his body develops sores and ulcers that extend from the neck down to the internal organs, causing him pain. He must take medicine and drink milk for the affliction to be removed and for him to recover. His parents think of him with concern and rejoice that he has attained healing.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is the father of the entire world; he manifests illness in order to eliminate the afflictions of all beings and cause them to attain peace and security.
When people hear that [the Buddha] has residual karmic retribution, they dare not commit further transgressions. This is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva.
He further addressed the Bodhisattva Hui-shang:

"In times long past, when people did not understand the nature of transgression and merit, the Tathāgata manifested calamities and misfortunes for the sake of the multitude. Therefore, the Tathāgata has said:
'I am the Dharma King and cannot escape the consequences of my past offenses; how then could you, who are of a similar kind, ever escape calamity?'"
From this there is a saying: "The Tathāgata is forever free from any remaining karmic retribution.

It is like a person who has skillfully mastered the arts of writing, calculation, and accounting; wishing to instruct various children so that they may achieve proficiency, he knows nothing he cannot explain without hindrance. When the children see and hear him, they receive his instruction and gradually master the fundamentals.

The Tathāgata is likewise; he has studied all dharmas without exception and possesses universal erudition, yet he manifests residual karmic retribution in order to cause sentient beings to be endowed with the pure Dharma.

It is like a physician who has newly begun to study the treatment of illnesses; understanding prescriptions and mastering medicines, he provides relief according to each ailment. Having been able to cure himself, he is further able to cure others on a vast scale, and thus he exclaims with admiration.
During the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there were five hundred merchants in that world who went to sea to seek jewels.

Among them was one of divergent mind whose mental transgression was extremely grave; he opened the gateway to sin, becoming a master of evil arts and a fierce thief intent on causing harm. Observing the appearance of the merchants, he saw that they were already upon the ship.
At that time, the leader was named Śrīdatta; he protected the merchants by monitoring them according to the circumstances.
The wicked man thought to himself:
"Now, why should I not kill all these merchants and take the treasures for myself alone?"
"In Jambudvīpa there was a great guide named Mahākāruṇika.
At that time, while he was asleep in a dream, the ocean deity spoke to him:
'Among the merchants, there is one thief who has conceived a great evil intent; he wishes to endanger and drown all five hundred merchants, desiring to seize the treasure for himself alone.'"
Even if this undertaking were to result in immeasurable sin, why is that?

These five hundred merchants have all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and right path and established themselves in non-retrogression; even if they were to meet with death, their resolve would not waver. By virtue of their merit, each and every bodhisattva will attain the unsurpassed, true, and right path, while the bandits shall fall into hell, where they must remain for many years until their transgressions are finally exhausted.
Now, O Benevolent Guide, you should employ skillful means so that this person shall not undergo the manifold sufferings of hell, and so that these merchants shall not be subjected to harm.
He reflected for seven days, finding no other means, and thought to himself:
"I must take him and endanger his life!
If I were to speak of this to the merchants, they would all become enraged; they would surely kill this man, and he would certainly fall into an evil rebirth."
Again he thought to himself:
"Even if I were to kill alone, I would still have to suffer the retribution; I would rather endure it myself.
Even if I must undergo the torments of hell for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, I will not allow these merchants to face universal peril, nor will I let this single thief fall into hell."
Then the Great Compassionate Teacher preached the Dharma for him, causing his heart to be joyful and exultant as he lay down to sleep.
The Buddha said, “Noble son!
That great leader, out of great compassion for the multitude of merchants, used skillful means to take the life of one thief.
After his life ended, he was reborn in the twelfth heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The Great Compassionate Teacher at that time was none other than myself; by means of this skillful expedient, I transcended birth and death for a thousand kalpas, and upon death, ascended to heaven.
As for the five hundred merchants on the same ship, they are those who will appear as the five hundred Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa.

How could a bodhisattva have any faults or afflictions? Having transcended and eliminated [suffering] from beginning to end for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one should not examine the Buddha and find him at fault; that which the Tathāgata manifests is solely for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, because of a deficiency, he provisionally manifested iron spikes; the Tathāgata stepped upon them, reaching them through his majestic spiritual power. Why is this?
Because the body of the Tathāgata is adamantine (*vajra*).
Furthermore, son of good family!
In the city of Śrāvastī there were twenty men who, in turn, had become enemies of another twenty men.
At that time, each of the first twenty men desired to seize their enemies and bring them harm, seeking every opportunity to watch for their chance in their final encounter.
Those twenty men, wishing to harm their twenty enemies, followed the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and immediately approached the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested forty people, also desiring to exhort the entire great assembly, and addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Now, at this very spot, an iron spike shall spontaneously emerge and enter the big toe of the Buddha’s right foot."
Before he had finished speaking, the iron stake appeared before the Buddha.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have now extracted this iron stake and placed it in another world-system."
The Buddha said, "It is not so.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, by the power of his diligence, sought to pull out the iron stake; however, this trichiliocosm shook violently, yet he could not move the stake even as much as a hair.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded toward the Brahma Heaven, and Vajra followed him immediately;
when the Tathāgata sat down, Vajra stood before him.
Then the Tathāgata took Vajra in his right hand and stepped upon it with his foot.
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
"Does the Tathāgata incur calamity because of past offenses?
The Buddha then told him:

"In the past, I entered the great ocean together with five hundred merchants. At that time, there was one man who harbored evil intentions; I killed him then, and this is the remaining retribution of that act."
When the twenty men heard the Buddha speak these words, they said to one another:

"If even the Tathāgata, the Dharma King who has attained sovereign mastery, still possesses residual karmic retribution that cannot be extinguished, how much more so for us, who have not yet escaped our offenses?"
They immediately came to the Buddha to repent and confess their transgressions.

The Tathāgata, in accordance with the occasion, preached the Dharma for them, distinguishing between demerit and merit, causing forty people to enter the wisdom of equality and thirty-two thousand people to attain the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement.
Because of this, the Tathāgata manifested an iron pin; this too is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"For what reason, World-Honored One, have you who are already free from all ailments manifested illness, causing the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, to compound medicinal decoctions?"

At that time, the Buddha had established two hundred and fifty precepts. Not long after, five hundred bhikṣus were practicing the path among the trees; as they neared the completion of their practice, doubt arose in their minds:
"The Tathāgata has given this instruction: 'One should treat all bodily ailments with only a single medicine and must not employ others.'"
At that time, the Buddha had this thought:
"By what skillful means can I enable the bhikṣus to practice the use of other medicines? Why was this?

If the Tathāgata were to grant permission according to their wishes, then people of future generations would disparage the four noble precepts; therefore, the Tathāgata employs skillful means as a physician, entrusting the task to Jīvaka.
Then a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven spoke to the bhikṣu, saying: "O worthy ones!
You should seek further medicine; do not endanger your lives."
Then they said to one another:
"We would rather shatter our own bodies than violate the Buddha’s precepts.
The deva replied to the worthy ones:

"The Tathāgata is now the Dharma King; he has ordered that you cease using this minor medicine and seek other remedies, so that you may change what you have practiced and aspire to what you should take.

At that time, the bhikṣu was freed from doubt and hesitation; he then sought different medicines, his illness was immediately cured, and within seven days, day and night, he attained the Way of Non-attachment.
If the Tathāgata had not practiced the use of medicinal decoctions, these bhikṣus would not have attained liberation; it shall be the same in future ages as well.
Only when their bodies are at ease and secure do they attain the Way; this, too, is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
"Why is it that although the Tathāgata is universally endowed with all virtues, he enters villages to practice almsround and returns with an empty bowl?
The Tathāgata has no misfortune; rather, out of compassion, he observes future generations in the borderlands and remote regions, giving rise to pity and sorrow for them."
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who enters a commandery, kingdom, district, town, or village to wander for alms, yet due to his own meager merit, he receives nothing from his begging.
He thinks to himself:

"The Tathāgata’s merits are full and abundant, and his assembly of immeasurable blessings is vast; even when he went on alms-round, he would leave with an empty bowl. Since the roots of goodness we have planted are not extensive, how could we harbor resentment and abandon our practice by not begging?"
"Therefore, I shall go on my alms-round.
For this reason, he entered the city for alms and returned with an empty bowl.
It is further said:
"That Māra has transformed various brahmins and householders to prevent them from making offerings to the Buddha or bestowing alms upon the Sangha—this has never happened before.
That Māra Pāpīyān did not dare to exert his power to harass and obstruct the Tathāgata or to thwart their intention for merit; this was a manifestation of the Buddha’s holy intent."
The brahmin householder harbored such a strange thought; it was not his original intention, nor was it due to the Buddha’s lack of merit.

At that time, when no one among the multitude had offered anything, and seeing the Tathāgata departing with an empty bowl, the devas and humans of the Māra realm perceived that the World-Honored One would receive no meal. They wondered whether the Blessed One might harbor a sense of despondency, and they focused their minds single-mindedly day and night, thinking that the Tathāgata and his assembly of disciples would surely fall into grief and distress.

Seeing that the disciples of the Buddha remained unchanged in heart—neither increasing nor decreasing—and were equal before and after, seventy thousand devaputras threw themselves before the Buddha; the Tathāgata, according to their needs, preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. This, too, is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why is it that Ciñcā Māṇavikā tied a wooden bowl to her belly to slander the Tathāgata?

This was not the lingering retribution for past deeds of the World-Honored One; rather, the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power was able to seize her violent intent and transport her beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The Tathāgata manifested this skillful means through his expedient power."

In the future, there may be bhikṣus who have left the household life to practice as śramaṇas and are slandered by others, causing them to harbor doubts. Even when they witness such derision and mockery directed at the Buddha, the World-Honored One, their minds remain unmoved and they do not reject the consequences of past karma, reflecting:
"The universal and supreme virtue of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, remains thus even now."
"How much more so for us, that we should not engage in criticism.
Having reflected thus, he redoubled his diligent effort; he purely upheld the precepts with a mind that did not waver.
Even if a violent intention were to slander him in a dream, after the end of his life, he would not escape hell.
The Tathāgata fully knows how to cause them to protect the prohibitions and precepts. Why is this?
Because the virtue of the Tathāgata does not abandon sentient beings; this is the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why did the followers of other paths harm Sudarśana and bury him among the *śiṃśapā* trees?
The Buddha, with his various supernormal knowledges and universal, unimpeded observation, knew that anger would arise; thus, he manifested such a display."
If one does not strike Sūdalī with a blade, Sūdalī might instead suffer from some other ailment.
The Buddha knew that the woman’s lifespan had come to an end; therefore, those of such a kind instructed her to kill her.

Regarding those who follow heterodox and deviant teachings, the harms they commit against themselves will inevitably result in retribution; the Buddha, through his impartial wisdom, transforms and establishes them, so that by means of what he thus establishes, the root of merit for all living beings is increased.
For this reason, the Tathāgata did not enter the city for seven days, during which time he transformed sixty billion devas and led them into the Way.

After the seven days had passed, the fourfold assembly all came to the Buddha to hear the Dharma; eighty-four thousand people attained the wisdom of equality, and three hundred million people realized the fruits of the path—those of the Stream-enterer, the Once-returner, and the Non-returner. This, too, was the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Why did the Tathāgata eat barley for three months?
The Tathāgata is fundamentally all-knowing; even when invited by a brahmin, he could not have failed to remember the transformative work the Buddha had undertaken."
Why is this so? These five hundred horses were formerly disciples of the Buddha.
After they had finished eating, they all studied the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva path in previous lives and made offerings to the World-Honored Ones of the past!
Following the instructions of evil friends, they committed numerous transgressions and fell into the realm of animals.

At that time, there were also five hundred horse trainers; there was a bodhisattva named Sūryagarbha who had originally made a vow to be born among them in order to universally transform such beings, causing them to resolve upon the Way and to propagate the Mahāyāna for the sake of all horse trainers.
Originally not a horse trainer, the Tathāgata protects them so that all the horses and livestock may receive their predictions of enlightenment.

For the sake of all Tathāgatas, who do not eat and have no personal desires, his majestic power can transform tiles, stones, swords, and staves into exquisite food and drink; everything within the trichiliocosm becomes sweet delicacies of extraordinary flavor.

Why is this so? Because the World-Honored One naturally possesses the mark of a great man and the sense of supreme flavor; therefore, one should know that all food and drink transformed by the Tathāgata are delicious.
The elder Ānanda, not yet having attained great compassion, thought to himself:
"How is it that the World-Honored One has abandoned the food of a wheel-turning monarch and now consumes barley?

The Buddha, knowing his thought, [manifested] the virtue of five hundred horse trainers; at that time, the five hundred horses all recognized their past lives and attained a mind close to the Way. Five hundred bodhisattvas, moved by great kindness and compassion, went to visit the Tathāgata. The five hundred horse trainers reduced their own rations by half to provide for the Buddha, while they surrendered the grain of the five hundred horses to provide for the five hundred bhikṣus.

The horse trainer and the horses all repented their transgressions. After three months had passed since they had seen the Buddha and the assembly of monks, five hundred horses reached the end of their lives and were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where they were honored by the devas. As was appropriate for them, they preached the Dharma and attained the stage of non-retrogression, destined to achieve the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
When Ānanda learned that such offerings had been bestowed, those within the palace experienced what they had never known before and came to address the Buddha, saying:
"We have grown up within the depths of this inner palace."
“World-Honored One!
Ānanda has never before experienced such peaceful joy as this, and he has not eaten for seven days.
“Noble son! [the Buddha replied.]

You should know that the body of the Tathāgata is free from any transgression or calamity; it is because there may be those in future generations who uphold the precepts yet invite śramaṇas without providing offerings that he manifests himself for their sake.
This is because when the Tathāgata is invited by someone, even if that person fails to provide the necessary offerings, he does not cause them to fall into a state of transgression.

Furthermore, for three months during the summer retreat, five hundred bhikṣus were with the Tathāgata; among them, four hundred bhikṣus possessed lustful dispositions and lacked pure thoughts. Had they obtained fine food, their lustful intentions would have increased; however, because they consumed coarse food, their lustful minds became thin, and within those three months, they were able to attain arhatship.

The Tathāgata manifests these learned bhikṣus and transformed bodhisattvas according to the occasion; this is not a transgression or calamity, but rather the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
"Why did the Tathāgata say to Mahākāśyapa, 'You should preach the sūtra; my back and waist ache'?
At that time, there were eight thousand devaputras who had originally practiced as disciples under Kāśyapa’s guidance."

At that time, those gathered there who delighted in and looked up to the Triple Gem, and who were diligent in their practice upon hearing the discourse on the *bodhicitta*, would not have been able to understand it even if ten billion Buddhas had preached the Dharma for them; only the bhikṣu Kāśyapa was able to deliver them!

Therefore, the Buddha told them to discern the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*). When eight thousand devaputras heard this teaching and attained wisdom, those who were ill went to the assembly to listen to the sutra, each thinking to themselves:
"The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, has caused our illnesses to be cured simply by speaking of the factors of awakening; why should we not listen to the sutra?"
"For what reason?
O son of good family!
Desiring to cause the various devas and the sick bhikṣu to receive and uphold the Way of the Sūtra, the Tathāgata manifested a backache; therefore, he said:"
"Kāśyapa’s preaching of the sūtra has caused my illness to be removed.
This, too, is the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"For what reason did the Tathāgata suffer a headache when the Śākya kingdom was destroyed?"
All the people thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata’s kinsmen shall not exhaust their lifespans.
With the intention of protecting the common people, he sat beneath a withered tree and addressed his attendant, saying:
"I have a severe headache.

At that time, there were three thousand deities who believed in permanence gathered in the assembly, along with an incalculable multitude of Kṣatriyas. Hearing the report that Ānanda suffered from the affliction of a headache, they thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata still has residual karmic retribution remaining."
“Upon hearing this sutra, seven thousand devas and humans were immediately transformed; this too was the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

For what reason did the brahmin Pāṭha revile the World-Honored One with five hundred matters, and the Buddha remained silent? Later, when he further praised the Buddha, the Buddha likewise remained silent.”
If, at that time, one takes refuge in oneself with single-minded repentance and remains silent,
the Buddha can suppress them so they do not speak further, casting them away and placing them in a different land.

At that time, among the countless multitudes of devas and worldlings in the assembly, having seen the Buddha’s power of patience, his wisdom-force, and his mind of equanimity—gentle, refined, and harmonious—four thousand people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

The Tathāgata perceives clearly that there are those to be transformed in the future; therefore, he manifests silence. This is not due to any remaining karmic retribution from the Buddha, but is rather the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Son of good family!..."

Listen. That which is produced by Devadatta constantly harasses and harms the Bodhisattva; harboring a mind of resentment and hatred, he seeks to injure him. This, too, is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Hui-shang:
"When the various devas come and go seeking something, this constitutes the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) in its vast and complete form. Why is this so? Because..."
Bringing great benefit and fulfilling all vows, they initiate everything.
By what causes and conditions do they give rise to such conduct?

If sentient beings were to dwell in peace and purity for their own self-interest, they would not understand giving nor know the recipient. For this reason, the devas manifest and come from the void to the place where the Bodhisattva dwells, testing him by requesting his wife and children, his head, eyes, hands, and feet, as well as his kingdom, cities, and villages.
At that time, the Bodhisattva fulfilled all desires with courageous wisdom and without difficulty.
When the multitude saw him, they emulated his practice of giving; they honored what he practiced without any stinginess or parsimony, saying:

"We too shall make vows to seek Buddhahood, cultivate the prohibitive precepts without daring to violate or lose them, and follow the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas without ever deviating or abandoning it."

To not feel resentment when struck or reviled, and not harbor hatred when treated with contempt, is the expansion of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). By means of this, he teaches and transforms immeasurable multitudes.

When various devas and humans see an enemy approaching, they go to the place where the Tathāgata is; thus their precepts and prohibitions are lengthened. This too is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Tathāgata, and not the result of other calamities or transgressions.
Why is this so? Those who dare to come and test him do so through skillful means (*upāya*).
Upon investigation, they all lead and benefit countless people. To state the essential point: there remain ten calamities manifested by the Tathāgata.
You should all know that the Buddha employs skillful means according to the times.
Because the masses harbor evil and mostly honor what is contrary to the Dharma, he manifests these responses for their sake; there is no calamity therein.

He causes them to know how to renounce [the world] and proceed toward supreme wisdom. That which the Tathāgata praises as the most honored skillful means is entirely free from calamity or transgression; it is merely a manifestation!
By acting thus, one attains this; those who hear it will be struck with awe and dare not commit evil.
Furthermore, son of good family!

This is proclaimed widely through skillful means and is spoken only at certain times; it is not for those who are dull-witted or of meager merit, nor is it a discourse known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Because they have never studied skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); only the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas understand and penetrate them deeply.
It is like lighting a fire inside a house on a dark night, which illuminates the entire interior for the wife, children, and kinsmen.

In this way, when a bodhisattva hears of the perfection of skillful means (upāyakauśalya-pāramitā), they will thoroughly understand all the practices of a bodhisattva; they should diligently and compliantly study that which I have practiced from the beginning.
The Buddha charges you:
"O son of good family!
O daughter of good family!"

If one seeks the Buddha-way and there is someone who expounds skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one should travel even a hundred or a thousand *li* to receive instruction from them, and thus one will receive the light. Why is this so?
"If one is able to hear and accept such a teaching as this, they shall illuminate all the sutras, severing the net of doubts so that no resentment remains.
At that time, the devas, worldly people, and the fourfold assembly all exclaimed in praise:
"As for those who hear this sūtra of skillful means, many who are not vessels for the Dharma will neither believe nor rejoice in it."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, seventy-two thousand people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named?"
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The name of this sutra is 'The Chapter on the Infinite Skillful Means for Delivering Others According to the Occasion.'"
"You should uphold it!
You should practice it!
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Hui-shang, the assembly of bhikṣus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the devas, nāgas, asuras, and humans were all filled with joy.
The Sūtra on the Great Skillful Means Spoken by the Buddha, Questioned by the Bodhisattva Prajñottara, Scroll II.
